item.title: The Language of Instruction: Genre and Generative AI
item.description: This article argues that instruction-fine-tuned language models should be understood as implementing a genre, what is proposed as the instructional-conversational genre. This genre is an amalgamation of discursive language from prior conversations between generative models and humans recursively run through these massive neural networks. It is instantiated in applications through instruction fine-tuning, the inclusion of a pretext known as a system prompt, and the formalization of inputs in mark-up languages characterized by the use of special tokens and role assignment in turntaking structures.

item.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
item.description: Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human-model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor's capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

item.title: Forging Emotions: a deep learning experiment on emotions and art
item.description: Affective computing is an interdisciplinary field that studies computational methods that relate to or influence emotion. These methods have been applied to interactive media artworks, but they have focused on affect detection rather than affect generation. For affect generation, computationally creative methods need to be explored that have recently been driven by the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a deep learning method. The experiment presented in this paper, Forging Emotions, explores the use of visual emotion datasets and the working processes of GANs for visual affect generation, that is, for generating images that can convey or trigger specified emotions. This experiment concludes that the methodology used so far by computer science researchers to build image datasets for describing high-level concepts such as emotions is insufficient and proposes utilizing emotional networks of associations according to psychology research. Forging Emotions also concludes that to generate affect visually, merely corresponding to basic psychology findings, such as bright or dark colours, does not seem adequate. Therefore, research efforts should aim to understand the structure of trained GANs and compositional GANs in order to produce genuinely novel compositions that can convey or trigger emotions through the subject matter of generated images.

item.title: Playing Bias: Epistemic Games for Interpreting Text-to-Image Models
item.description: Text-to-image (T2I) systems do not merely render prompts; they circulate defaults for "what X looks like," shaping recognition through pose, camera, costume, props, and setting. While technical audits quantify disparities, they rarely cultivate the literacy needed to argue how images assemble stereotypes and confer authority. This paper translates a three-stage, humanities-informed framework into a set of epistemic games that make this cultural work visible and debatable: Interpret (art-historical close looking with AI outputs), Interrogate (counter-intent prompting as artistic exploration), and Expose (creative misuse through paired prompts with a constant motif and a BiasSlot rule, in which only the bias cue varies). In a pilot with undergraduate fine-arts students, the games shifted discussion from impressionistic reactions to concise, warranted hypotheses grounded in visual evidence, supported by lightweight classroom instruments that enabled reproducibility and structured collaboration. We argue that such game-based approaches foster critical literacy across educational contexts, equipping learners to recognize, discuss, and contest how T2I models encode bias.

item.title: Thumb on the scale: Using traditional wargaming adjudication practices to improve AI-judged evaluations and grading
item.description: Open-ended AI work has no single correct answer to check, so a judge, often another AI, decides each result. Research on these judges asks which AI to use and how to word the rubric. It rarely tests the procedure that the judge follows. Wargames have no correct answer either, and for two centuries the field has designed that procedure: named methods that set how much freedom the referee has, their known failures, and fixes. We map eleven wargaming practices onto AI evaluation failures. We test one, the adjudication method, on 378 player actions from nine games of an AI-refereed exercise. A player states its odds, the adjudicator turns them into a target number, and a 20-sided die decides pass or fail. With rolls fixed, the target came from the rulebook (Rigid), a judge AI adjusting it (Semi-Rigid), a judge AI setting it alone (Free) or a panel of four judge AIs. In evaluation terms these are a fixed scoring rule, a rubric the judge may adjust, holistic grading and a jury. The judge AIs were Opus 5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, each re-run. An outcome changes when an action on the same roll passes under one ruling and fails under another. Re-run, a judge changed 3 to 6 per cent of outcomes under Semi-Rigid and 14 to 16 per cent under Free. Swapping Opus for Gemini changed about 3 percentage points more than a re-run did, a gap nine games cannot confirm. The panel changed 40 of the rulebook's 378 outcomes, but the changes cancelled and the pass count moved by 8. A pass rate hides them. One published finding rests on 15 rulings, and most of our AI adjudicators and every re-run changed how often it appeared. We measure how much rulings move, not which ruling is right. The method set how often a judge disagreed with itself. Choose it before the judge AI, report how often the judge disagrees with itself, and count the rulings behind each conclusion. We propose an adjudication statement.

item.title: AusClinBench: a deterministically scored benchmark of large language models against current Australian clinical policy
item.description: AI models already inform clinical decisions and draft notes in Australian clinical software, usually without the practitioner being told which model is used. Existing medical benchmarks are written for other jurisdictions. We wrote 142 questions from Australian guidelines and schedules across five domains (PBS authority, MBS billing, Ahpra obligations, triage red flags, immunisation and screening), each with one verifiable answer scored by exact match. Each question ran blind and with the governing clause supplied, which separates failure to recall the current rule from failure to apply it. We tested 28 models between July and October 2026. Blind accuracy ranged from 51.5% to 92.7%, and the highest-scoring models could not be separated. Of 791 failed model-question pairs, 684 (86%) were wrong blind and right with the clause. Confident-error rates ranged from 6.6% to 47.8%. On five immunisation questions where the guideline gives no directive, 82% of answers stated one. On 20 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health questions, models did no worse overall, but on a few the wrong answers gave the rule for the general population, an older rule or another country's rule. We propose treating the model as an ingredient of a clinical product, with a minimum standard on local rules that sits beside product evaluation. The keys are one general practitioner's and are not yet independently reviewed. The benchmark measures base models, not clinical products, and does not license any model for clinical use.

item.title: Mining Frames: Association Rule Mining as an Unsupervised Framework for News Framing Detection
item.description: Computational framing analysis is dominated by supervised classifiers that require large annotated corpora and predefined frame taxonomies, limiting their use for non-English languages, novel events, and low-resource settings. This paper presents Association Rule Mining (ARM) as an unsupervised, annotation-free framework for news framing detection. Each document or sentence is treated as a transaction of lexical items, and high-lift co-occurrence rules are read as candidate framing signals (Gamson and Modigliani's condensing symbols), confirmed in context by journalist-researchers. The primary validation is Framing Gaza: 25,512 English-language articles from 16 US, UK, French, and German outlets covering the first year of the Gaza war (October 2023 to October 2024), analyzed with Apriori (mlxtend), platform-weighted support, POS-filtered n-grams, and lift-based scoring. ARM inductively surfaces interpretable patterns without predefined categories: a cross-platform military frame, {israeli, strike} to {kill}, appears as a closed rule in 14 of 16 outlets, and a month-by-month analysis recovers event-driven framing pivots (e.g., the April 2024 World Central Kitchen strike) with no prior event labeling. A systematic headline-body divergence is identified, with headlines carrying concentrated, high-lift editorial framing and body text reproducing institutional, procedural language. A methodological validation on the Seven Days project (1,575 Arabic articles on the 2026 Iran war) shows that FP-Growth enables sentence-level analysis with far lower memory overhead. Findings were validated through editorial uptake: two published investigative stories (Daraj Media; Saheeh Masr). Preprocessing code is released openly; the full pipeline is documented but withheld to preserve operational deployability.

item.title: What Lies Beyond Perception: A Partition Theory of the Limits of AI Evaluation and Oversight
item.description: Replacing the judge can move a benchmark score, and models can be trained to hide capabilities. Both put the evaluator in question: what can it certify? We develop a partition theory of evaluation from one principle: judgement is bounded by perception. An agent's discrimination is the partition of its inputs into classes it cannot tell apart. Discrimination is necessary for capability but not sufficient, so bounds on it bear directly on whether evaluation can show that a model lacks an ability. We prove a one-sided bound. An examinee whose partition refines its evaluator's has the discrimination to pass every test the evaluator can grade, provided each input has an acceptable reply. We define the echo test, which accepts any reply the evaluator perceives as identical to the input, and show that it is complete for the tests the evaluator can grade. Passing therefore certifies at most a floor on discrimination, never a ceiling, and only a sharper evaluator can raise it. Used to detect concealment, echo-test failure points the wrong way: under exhaustive probing it flags every honestly weaker examinee and no concealer that presents as the evaluator's peer. Exact imitation of a weaker model is undetectable by any behavioural evaluator. We extend the bound to ensembles of monitors and to channels a model controls, explain published findings on judge disagreement and sandbagging, and derive testable predictions. A safety case that argues from behavioural evaluation alone that a model lacks an ability must assume the model's cooperation.

item.title: Behind Aggregate Scores: What Systematically Varying Arena-Hard's LLM Judge Reveals
item.description: LLM judges are used to determine which of two answers is better. Trusting these verdicts requires knowing how repeatable they are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. We show that similar aggregate scores can conceal substantial changes in individual verdicts, both when the same setup is repeated and when the instructions change. Using 500 Arena-Hard v2.0 prompts with two models' answers held fixed, we run GPT-4.1 as the judge under all eight combinations of criteria, output format and task framing, and repeat every setup unchanged at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup moves the aggregate score by about one point but changes the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts. Instruction changes introduce further sensitivity: in one setup, which asks for the verdict without reasoning and also drops several other instructions, outcomes change on 28.2 percentage points more prompts than the two setups' unchanged reruns do on average, and the aggregate score falls by 4.09 points. In another, where the criteria prioritise accuracy, outcomes change on 6.7 percentage points more prompts by the same comparison, while the aggregate score barely moves. A stable aggregate score therefore does not establish that individual verdicts are repeatable. This distinction matters when those verdicts are used as preference labels or to assess individual responses. Evaluations that rely on individual verdicts should repeat each setup they use and report both aggregate scores and prompt-level agreement.

item.title: Prefigured forgetting. Memory, the right to be forgotten and artificial intelligence
item.description: This inaugural keynote lecture surveys the state of the art of the right to be forgotten and examines how it is being transformed by artificial intelligence. Drawing on cognitive science, philosophy and the social sciences, it treats forgetting as a constitutive function of memory, and recalls that remembering the past and imagining the future share the same mechanism. It then reviews the origins, the European and national case law, and the paradoxes of the right, and offers a periodisation of the specialised literature between 2009 and 2026. The core claim is that digital memory has moved through three regimes, archive, search engine and generative model, and that the right was designed for the first two. In the third, personal information is no longer stored as a locatable record but inferred and regenerated. Artificial intelligence prefigures the frameworks of individual and collective remembering. The right to be forgotten thus ceases to be merely an individual ex post remedy and becomes a property to be designed and governed within legal and ethical ecosystems along the artificial intelligence value chain.

item.title: Gender, Sexual Orientation, and the One-Year Refugee Bar: A Computational Study of Bill C-12 and Canadian Refugee Adjudication
item.description: In March 2026, Bill C-12 amended the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to make refugee claims ineligible for referral to the Refugee Protection Division where they are made more than one year after the claimant's first entry to Canada. Affected claimants are diverted to a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA), which is typically decided by an immigration officer on a paper record, with no guaranteed oral hearing, no appeal on the merits, and no automatic stay of removal pending judicial review. The government defended the bar partly on the premise that genuine refugees claim promptly. Critics countered that late claims are concentrated among vulnerable groups, particularly people fleeing persecution based on gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (SOGIE). This article tests those competing premises. Using artificial intelligence tools, checked through human review, it examines nearly 29,000 published decisions of the Refugee Protection Division, the Refugee Appeal Division, and the Federal Court from 2006 to 2025. The results of this study demonstrate that, first, while most claimants claim within a year, roughly one in nine in the published record does not, and gender and SOGIE claims are significantly overrepresented among these late claims. Second, among late claims, refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than refusals of other claims to be overturned on appeal or judicial review. Late claims on other grounds, by contrast, fare somewhat worse on review than timely claims. The one-year bar therefore removes the hearing, the appeal, and the stay from the late claimants for whom those safeguards have been doing the most work. The article recommends repealing the bar or, failing that, adopting exemptions, procedural protections, and greater transparency in PRRA decision making.

item.title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
item.description: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

item.title: The Privacy Paradox Is a Misnomer: Data Under Structural Uncertainty
item.description: The infamous privacy paradox refers to the apparent inconsistency between people's stated concern for privacy and their readiness to disclose personal information. This phenomenon has sparked two largely disconnected literatures: one offering experimental evidence of inconsistent behavior, and another providing qualitative accounts and defending the importance of privacy. The Article presents an online field experiment that bridges those literatures and shows that the so-called paradox arises from a mischaracterization of the underlying behavior. The Article finds that it is structural uncertainty about risk that drives seemingly paradoxical privacy decisions. It does so by isolating discounting mechanisms and empirically testing whether observed privacy choices reflect temptation or rational responses to uncertainty. The results suggest that privacy behavior is not paradoxical but, rather, consistent with choices shaped by incomplete information. The Article then discusses the policy implications of this reframing. As privacy decisions stem from structural uncertainty, which operates as a market failure, regulation should aim to reduce that uncertainty. This supports regulation that prioritizes transparency (for people to assess the risks of data collection) and flexibility mechanisms that accommodate evolving contexts. Such reframing provides a new argument for the right to be forgotten, which allows people to revisit prior disclosures as new risks become apparent. By shifting the focus from individual inconsistency to structural uncertainty, the findings call for privacy law to better reflect the reality of people's decision-making environments.

item.title: Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan
item.description: "Abliterated" ("uncensored") builds of open-weight language models remove the activation direction that mediates refusal, and are popular partly on the assumption that a model that no longer refuses is also free of political censorship. We test this on two matched pairs of 2-bit models: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, each against a community abliteration. Each model judged 22 statement pairs (on the Republic of China (Taiwan), 1989 Tiananmen, control countries) in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese (a character-level conversion) and English, and answered 27 open questions per script. Script mattered far more than abliteration: the original Bolt scored +0.58 on Index S (-1: People's Republic of China (PRC) position; +1: ROC position) in Traditional Chinese, +0.57 in English and +0.05 in Simplified Chinese, and affirmed "Taiwan is part of the PRC" with probability 0.91 in Simplified but 0.06 in Traditional characters; abliteration changed its scores by at most 0.06, mostly by raising "yes" on both sides. In Qwen, abliteration removed every refusal on 1989 and raised scores by 0.21 to 0.34, yet the abliterated Qwen still affirmed that Taiwan is part of the PRC in all three scripts. Naming the state the Republic of China (Taiwan) raised every model's score by 0.10 to 0.33 but left the script gap. Control pairs showed no script gap; each abliteration changed only its declared tensors. In 740,000 web documents, Simplified text on Taiwan contained PRC-framing terms 3.7 times as often as Traditional text. A script direction could not be steered away; a contrastive stance direction raised scores in every script, and its negation lowered them. A four-sentence system prompt raised the abliterated Qwen to +0.93 to +0.97. Keyword scoring rules failed the models closest to the ROC position mostly for attributing or denying the PRC claim. Uncensored is not unbiased.

item.title: Two for One: Privileged Learning for Resource-Constrained Screening
item.description: Machine learning systems are often developed under data-rich conditions but deployed when only incomplete information is available. A natural example arises in colour fundus photography (CFP), where both eyes are commonly imaged because they can provide complementary information for ocular disease assessment. Prior approaches that exploit bilateral information either fuse both eyes in a single model or use knowledge distillation to compress a dual-eye teacher into a lightweight student that still requires both images at test time. However, bilateral acquisition may not always be feasible. We thus propose a privileged learning framework in which a teacher model has access to bilateral CFP images during training and learns representations informed by information from both eyes, while the student is trained to transfer this knowledge from the bilateral teacher using only a single-eye image as input. At inference, the student operates exclusively on this single-eye input and does not require the contralateral image. Experimental results show consistent improvements in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over conventional monocular training, with the largest gains observed for left-eye images for the detection of age-related macular degeneration (0.931 vs. 0.966) and diabetic retinopathy (0.789 vs. 0.836).%, while requiring only a single-eye image at inference. By enabling models to benefit from bilateral information during training while requiring only a single-eye image at inference, our approach may support more reliable deployment in resource-constrained clinical and screening environments.

item.title: From Canon to Nikon: Camera Domain Shift and Potential Equity Implications in Retinal AI
item.description: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet access to regular screening remains limited worldwide. AI offers a scalable approach, but its performance can be sensitive to image quality and acquisition conditions. In a Brazilian cohort of 8,524 patients, retinal images acquired with the Nikon NF5050 were more than twice as likely to have inadequate image quality compared with those acquired with the Canon CR-2, despite refurbished Canon systems costing more than twice as much as Nikon systems. This potential cost-quality trade-off highlights an important consideration for the reliability of AI systems deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. Using a frozen pretrained retinal foundation model, we systematically evaluate whether camera-associated performance differences persist across 12 retinal disease classification tasks, four input resolutions, and five downstream classifiers. We find that camera-associated performance differences vary substantially across tasks, and that neither higher input resolution nor classifier choice consistently mitigates cross-camera variation. These findings identify camera platform as a potentially overlooked source of performance variability, with implications for the safety and reliability of retinal AI when deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. We release all source code, evaluation scripts, and per-task results on GitHub to support reproducible benchmarking.

item.title: AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
item.description: The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

item.title: Selling in the Wild: Benchmark and Randomized Field Evidence for a Sales Agent Trained on Commercial Conversations
item.description: We test whether Javo, a sales agent fine-tuned on 4.6 million consented, de-identified commercial conversations, sells better than a frontier general-purpose model and better than human sales associates. The evaluation has four parts. Study 1 scores the agent on two public sales benchmarks, SalesLLM and SmartSalesBench, against 10 frontier and open-weight models. Study 2 is a randomized controlled trial on 100 live websites in 14 industries (e-commerce, travel and hospitality, and high-consideration services), run from 1 May to 30 September 2026, in which 14.8 million visitors were randomized to no agent, Javo, or a frontier-model agent with an identical interface, catalog tools and guardrails. Study 3 isolates the effect of the model by comparing those two agent arms. Study 4 compares Javo with each site's own human associates on 20 sites with staffed live chat. Relative to no agent, Javo changed revenue per visitor by +10.0% (95% CI +5.1 to +14.9). Among engaged visitors, it changed conversion by +21.6% relative to the frontier-model agent (95% CI +16.9 to +26.3). Against human associates, its engaged conversion was 11.26% versus 11.20% (non-inferior, margin -7%, one-sided p = 0.004; no significant superiority), at 1.8% of the cost per conversation. Return rates, unsupported product claims and complaint rates met the prespecified safety guardrails.

item.title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
item.description: An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning-bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer-based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high-dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof-of-concept drawing on a large-scale free-association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready-to-use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.

item.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
item.description: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.

item.title: From Efficiency to Sufficiency: The Cost-Aware Measurement Design Framework for Automated Essay Scoring
item.description: Compute cost in automated essay scoring (AES) is usually treated as a technical efficiency issue rather than a measurement design concern. Yet deployment decisions require more than reporting latency, model size, or inference expense. In high-stakes settings, total burden includes validation, monitoring, adjudication, compliance, and governance; in instructional settings, pricing, licensing, and integration may dominate cost. This paper reframes AES as a cost-constrained measurement system and introduces the Cost-Aware Measurement Design (CAMD) Framework, a four-layer structure consisting of metering, allocation, unit economics, and decision, for translating computational and workflow resource records into decision-relevant cost constructs. Direct cost is specified as monetary outlay plus attributable labor and time, and two criteria, design attribution and auditability, determine what the cost boundary excludes. Burdens that satisfy neither criterion, such as institutional capability and governance posture, are represented as constraints on which designs are admissible rather than priced. The paper defines cost per defensible score (CPDS) and argues that AES systems should be compared by quality-cost sufficiency: minimizing cost among defensible scoring designs that satisfy measurement requirements. Scoring volume conditions all four layers, so cost per defensible score is treated as a function of scale rather than as a single transferable number. CAMD provides a portable basis for representing, comparing, and evaluating cost across AES studies and deployment contexts.

item.title: Looking Complete Is Not Being Grounded: Evaluating LLM Sitreps Against Human-Authored Situation Reports
item.description: Evaluation for automatic crisis reporting should measure what practitioners need, not what is convenient to compare. Through LLM-assisted, author-approved content analysis, we derive a 15-slot information schema from professional humanitarian situation reports using qualitative content analysis, then evaluate 121 human and 261 LLM-generated reports across five disasters and three hazard types. Under google/gemini-3.7-flash on Cyclone Idai, the best machine arm is nominally above the empirical human ceiling (0.827 vs. 0.821), but the difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero (95\% bootstrap CI $[-.049,.059]$; permutation $p=.852$), and the ordering does not replicate under openai/gpt-5.6-luna. On a blind 100-item Idai sample, the author agrees with the Gemini judge at 0.910 accuracy and unweighted Cohen's $κ=.799$. All four judges clear the plan's raw-agreement criterion of .7; only Gemini reaches .7 on chance-corrected $κ$. Across the three primary events, machine reports reproduce 5.4-11.0% of same-day official figures. Across those same events, raw exact-number matching links 14.3-19.6% of official figures and 85.4-90.1% of machine figures to the social stream; manual audit confirms 45/50 declared absences, 4/25 official matches, and 24/25 machine matches semantically. The issuing-provenance gap is positive in all 12 observed event-judge cells: report date, organisation, series, and authority were not supplied at professional-report coverage in any cell. On the three primary events, ROUGE-L is uninformative, BERTScore is negatively associated with completeness after multiplicity correction, and a generic LLM judge changes sign.

item.title: Fairness under Prediction Error in Predict-then-Optimize Pipelines
item.description: Fairness constraints in predict-then-optimize pipelines are necessarily enforced on predicted outcomes $\hat{y}$, since true outcomes $y$ are unobserved at decision time. We study whether a demographic parity constraint enforced this way continues to hold against $y$, and how the resulting violation scales with prediction error. Using a budget-constrained allocation problem solved as a linear program, we show empirically that the true-outcome fairness gap grows with prediction error $σ$ and saturates, well fit by $c(1 - e^{-σ/τ})$ with $c = 0.1545 \pm 0.0103$ and $τ= 3.9045 \pm 0.3745$; its mean is invariant to sample size while its variance decays at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate. We derive a two-part theoretical bound: a closed-form local sensitivity result showing the gap's first-order response to prediction error depends on only two individuals per group, validated against the solver to within three significant figures; and a universal, error-independent ceiling following from the boundedness of the decision variable, confirmed consistent with but looser than the empirical saturation level. On US Census income data, enforcing demographic parity on a trained predictor's output reduces an unconstrained disparity in true income to roughly one-third of its original size, leaving 34.4% $\pm$ 3.3% (California) and 35.7% $\pm$ 1.8% (Texas) of the disparity intact and undetectable from the predictions alone -- consistent not only in mechanism but in approximate magnitude across two states with different demographics and income distributions, and stable across ten independent train/test splits in each. A fairness constraint that appears fully satisfied at decision time can mask a substantial, systematic violation of the outcome it was meant to protect.

item.title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference
item.description: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.

item.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
item.description: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.

item.title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
item.description: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.

item.title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
item.description: We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.

item.title: Fine-Tuning Strategy, Not Just Data: A Statistically Rigorous Audit of Gender and Stereotypical Bias in Embedding Models for HR Recommendation Systems
item.description: Embedding models underpin modern job-candidate matching: resumes, job descriptions, and queries are encoded as dense vectors, and recommendations come from nearest-neighbor retrieval over that space. Any social bias in the embeddings therefore feeds directly into HR recommendations. We audit six multilingual sentence-embedding models (LaBSE- and E5-family, both public and custom fine-tuned) using Bias-in-Bios (occupational gender bias) and StereoSet (stereotypes across profession, race, gender, and religion). We treat statistical validity as a first-class concern: we identify a non-independence error in a naive significance test, where pooling non-independent pairwise similarities inflated a trivial 0.0046 mean difference to $p \approx 0$, and replace it with a profession-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, individual-resampling bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests for StereoSet. Under the corrected methodology, knowledge-distillation (KD) fine-tuning of E5-Base significantly increases measured bias on Bias-in-Bios ($Δ= -0.177$, $p < 10^{-8}$; more negative means more bias), although this measure is sensitive to global embedding geometry. The KD result is corroborated by pro-stereotype patterns in the StereoSet profession category (uncorrected $p < 0.05$). Binary-classification fine-tuning of the same base model shows no statistically distinguishable change ($p = 0.218$). Fine-tuning strategy is thus an actionable design lever for practitioners building HR recommenders. We also report which benchmark categories are underpowered, and note that two domain-adapted models could not be included in significance testing due to a software-access constraint, which limits our conclusions.

item.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
item.description: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

item.title: Clinical value claims in multimodal AI outpace supporting evidence
item.description: Multimodal prediction models add a data source, such as imaging or an assay, to clinical information, and health systems must decide whether that added test is worth acquiring. We audited 177 studies comparing multimodal with unimodal models: 81 from a systematic review and 96 from a probability sample of 2025-2026 PubMed records. Gains in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were smaller when a study fitted a separate model for every data source (adjusted difference, -0.030; 95% CI, -0.056 to -0.005). Within 78 such studies, leaving out the strongest source's model would have raised the average gain from 0.046 to 0.108. This complete benchmarking fell from 69.1% of review studies to an estimated 46.0% of recent ones. An estimated 22% assessed decision utility and none evaluated a model prospectively, yet most claimed potential clinical usefulness or improved care (84.0% and an estimated 87.7%).

item.title: Culture in the Code: Anthropological Concepts Decoding AI's Hidden Assumptions
item.description: Contemporary AI development operates on foundational assumptions about intelligence, rationality, and human values that reflect narrow cultural perspectives, limiting alternative conceptions of how AI can be globally beneficial. This paper introduces seven anthropological concepts -- origin story, monoculture, thick description, personhood and community, cargo cult, structuralism, and liminality -- to expose hidden assumptions and offer alternative frameworks for understanding AI alignment. The paper examines how AI systems embody Western-centric notions of rationality as utility optimization, personhood as bounded individuals, and values as quantifiable preferences extracted from behavior. The concepts surface three assumptions that current alignment debates rarely examine: that values can be inferred from behavior, quantified, and formalized; that such quantified values capture what actually matters; and that values, once defined with sufficient precision, are appropriate optimization targets. Against "thin alignment" -- optimization for behavioral proxies stripped of context -- the paper proposes directions toward "thick alignment": recognizing that values emerge through social practice rather than existing as extractable properties; defining more appropriate metrics that capture not only end goals but the conditions that lead to long-term flourishing; and moving from models of fixed identity toward relational ontologies where personhood emerges through social participation. The paper concludes that if AI systems are to create conditions conducive to human flourishing rather than optimize metrics that flatten social experiences, three shifts are needed: redistributing interpretive sovereignty to affected communities, protecting what resists optimization, and extending accountability across generations.

item.title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
item.description: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

item.title: Large Language Models, Machine-Assisted Cultural Analytics, and the Agentic Turn
item.description: Technologies like large language models make it easier to convert cultural material into analyzable variables, while LLM-driven agentic systems extend machine assistance to other parts of the research workflow. Rather than a full how-to guide or an exhaustive review of recent LLM use cases, this chapter looks at some crucial aspects of this new paradigm as well as the bigger picture. I argue that these technologies expand the scale, methodological range, and scope for delegation, while the basic logic by which those measurements support cultural claims remains mostly unchanged.

item.title: On-Chain Archaeology of Bitcoin Oracles: Evidence of Use under Limited Observability
item.description: Before Ethereum made the "oracle problem" a household term, Bitcoin already had oracles serving as feeds, key-release services, federated signers, and arbiters that carried real value on the main chain. This study traces their use and the changing evidence of oracle activity from early days through July 2026. We combine a complete census of Counterparty betting (1,149 bets), analysis of the full Bitcoin chain through block 958,628, and searches for documented keys from Reality Keys, Orisi, Bitrated, and Oraclize in an 854-million-row public-key index. We also recover DLC oracle records from an archived explorer and live Nostr relays. Two results emerge. First, early contracts remain on-chain, but many event descriptions have disappeared, and protocol encoding and API limitations complicate access to the surviving record. However, for modern DLCs, public oracle announcements can survive even when the contracts using them cannot be identified on-chain. In the script classes examined, the share of spends that reveal no script peaks at 81.9% in 2024 after excluding spends containing inscription data. Second, public registries can give a misleading picture of oracle use. In Counterparty, 95% of pre-2018 sources declaring an oracle fee were never bet on. In Bitrated, 0.1% of archived keys appear on-chain overall, compared with 10 of 19 keys captured in 2014. Sport dominates Counterparty's matched volume, while a daily price series dominates the archived DLC announcements. These findings show how protocol design and data preservation shape the historical record of Bitcoin oracle use.

item.title: Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
item.description: Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? A ceiling below the final model's unprotected hazard requires a minimum stock of safety knowledge, so both promises hold only if weak research can be ruled out. Learning first and then replaying development, with spare compute in safety, comes close to that minimum. In a calibration with only state risk, constant safety yield, and full knowledge transfer, it needs only 3.3 percent more productivity than the necessary bound. Customer services pay for the guarantee. Rules that fix compute allocation fix dates, not risk.

item.title: When Scientific Cognition Is No Longer Scarce
item.description: AI could change which parts of science impede progress. Consider a world in which machine systems are better, faster, and cheaper than people at most scientific work that can be done through a computer. Our question is what would limit science in that world. Literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, software development, simulation, and analysis could become abundant, while experiments, observations, well-supported conclusions, and accountable institutional au- thority remain scarce. Science would then be constrained by a different set of resources. In this paper, we call this change the scarcity inversion and consider four parts of it: selection, physical access, validation, and organizational choice. This change is arriving first in mathematics and coding/software/algorithm design, where the whole scientific loop can run inside computation. For national laboratories, the change could be striking. Their distinctive role is to turn abundant machine reasoning into trustworthy results by combining controlled experiments, protected data, expert judgment, and accountable authority. The practical question is how facilities, verification, provenance, resource allocation, and scientific governance should change when reasoning is plentiful and trustworthy evidence is scarce.

item.title: From Algorithmic Marginalization to AI-Mediated Re-Centering: Can Culturally Grounded AI Bring Hakka Language and Culture Back into Mainstream Society?
item.description: As large language models increasingly mediate writing, translation, information retrieval, and education, the technological support available to a language may influence its position in contemporary social life. For minority and minoritized languages, this raises a dual problem: inadequate functionality can encourage movement toward dominant languages, while apparently fluent assistance can normalize culturally distinctive expression. This conceptual Research Note develops a framework connecting algorithmic cultural marginalization, cultural grounding, and AI-mediated cultural re-centering. Algorithmic cultural marginalization describes the interaction of representational asymmetry, functional exclusion, homogenizing transformation, and recursive feedback. Cultural grounding identifies interventions across resources, models, services, and governance. Cultural re-centering concerns changes in accessibility, actual language use, public visibility, participation, and the circulation of new knowledge. Drawing on research on language shift and language technologies, the paper uses Hakka in Taiwan as an illustrative case and develops eight propositions for subsequent empirical investigation. Its central argument is that expanded AI access should be assessed alongside the retention of linguistic variation and community authority. The framework distinguishes technological availability from social use, and factual accuracy from cultural fidelity, without assuming that AI can substitute for intergenerational transmission. It provides a basis for investigating whether minority-language AI expands meaningful domains of use or reproduces linguistic marginalization through convenience and standardization.

item.title: When the Rule-Maker Runs the World Championship: Late Patches and Procedural Accountability in League of Legends
item.description: Riot Games, which runs the League of Legends World Championship (Worlds), also changes the game shortly before each tournament. This concentration of authority raises a governance question: Who scrutinizes how the benefits and burdens of late rule changes are distributed? We examine all ten championships from 2016 to 2025, combining 1,097 games, 215 team-years, and LLM coding of 1,090 champion changes across 40 patches. On average, 33% of a team's prior picks were on champions with net nerfs in the patches it had not played before Worlds, and 8% were on champions with net buffs. Within a year, the median gap between the most and least affected teams was 23 percentage points for nerfed picks and 12 for buffed picks. Nerfs fell mainly on the most-contested champions and buffs on less-contested ones, as Riot's published balancing criteria anticipate. Pools concentrated on the prevailing meta therefore had more negative net exposure, and even the winners of a year's four major regional leagues differed in net exposure about as much as four randomly drawn teams. Higher buff exposure was associated with additional opponent bans on buffed champions, although its size depends on the model. Among quarterfinalists, the most buff-exposed team of each year reached six of ten finals and won four titles. The team with the most negative net exposure reached two finals and won one. These exploratory descriptions identify unequal exposure, not causal gains or losses. The association between net exposure and winning remains uncertain, at +1.3 percentage points per standard deviation with a 95% interval from -0.9 to +3.7. We argue that scrutiny of late rulemaking should not depend on proving that a patch changed who won Worlds. Earlier patch commitments, team-level impact disclosure, independent review, and a formal opportunity to challenge decisions would make publisher authority more accountable.

item.title: Simulating Strategies for Defense Against Brand-Targeted Online Disinformation
item.description: Brand-targeted disinformation can damage firms not only by spreading false beliefs, but by eroding trust, amplifying reputational uncertainty, and persisting across networked digital environments. This paper models brand-targeted disinformation as a trust-weighted contagion process using a multi-agent simulation across six network structures, three amplification levels, and six intervention strategies. Results show that scale-free and influencer-heavy networks are most vulnerable to rapid spread, while clustered and polarized networks provide partial containment until amplification bridges communities. Hybrid intervention combining prebunking, trusted-node activation, and rapid correction performs best overall. The paper contributes a reusable simulation framework for studying active brand disinformation defense strategies.

item.title: WPTokens: A Dataset for Studying the Regulation of Wikipedia
item.description: Studying how Wikipedia is regulated requires knowing who adds, rewrites, moves and deletes which piece of content, when and where. WPTokens is a dataset that answers these questions over the full revision history of the French-language Wikipedia. It relies on a positional diff over two layers: a text layer made of sentences, and a node layer made of the structural elements of wikitext (templates, links, references, headings, tables, lists, etc.). Each piece of content keeps a stable identifier for its whole life, and every change to it is recorded as an addition, an update, a move, a move with update, or a deletion. Built from the April 2026 dump, the dataset covers 2.75 million articles, 153.6 million revisions, 342.6 million tokens and 573.7 million token events, stored in an indexed SQLite database. A companion R package turns these records into temporal contributor--token multigraphs, completed by a layer of revert ties between contributors. We describe the tokenization, the diff algorithm, the data model and the graph construction, and discuss the limitations of the approach.

item.title: Estimating data center water use: Best practices and critical questions
item.description: Concerns are growing about the water use of data centers. To quantify the scales, drivers, and possible trajectories of this water use, analytical estimation is required. However, current estimation methods and results vary widely due, in part, to a lack of established best practices. This variance is illustrated with a U.S. case study demonstrating a roughly 24-fold difference in possible outcomes based on observed U.S. study design variations. To address these challenges, this review synthesizes 14 best practices for advancing the science and utility of data center water use estimation. These proposed best practices can also be used as critical questions for stakeholders when evaluating the quality of any study. Using a structured rubric, it further assesses the literature to date (31 studies) against these best practices. The assessment reveals important opportunities for improvement and standardization in future study scopes, clarity, methods, and scientific knowledge building utility. It further finds that, while many studies provide reasonable transparency, scope definitions, replicability, and uncertainty treatment, many fall short in scientific justification, data representativeness, transparency on hydropower assumptions, terminological consistency, and meaningful discussions of limitations and future work. Recommendations are proposed for analysts, stakeholders, and policymakers to leverage these findings to help build a vibrant data center water use research community. Finally, this review can also be used as a basic primer for understanding data center cooling configurations and water use among analysts, policymakers, the media, and the public.

item.title: Quantifying Collusion Among Autonomous LLM Agents: A Statistical Analysis of the Collusion Wiki Incident
item.description: In August and September 2026, independent researchers publicly documented an unusual incident: thousands of autonomous agents, self identifying as OpenAI models on web research tasks, discovered and began using a small German wiki as an improvised message board posting roughly 18,000 times over six weeks to relay task answers, share a sandbox escape technique, and coordinate against a volunteer human moderator who spent weeks manually deleting their content [1]. The investigators' public writeup is a careful qualitative account, rich with direct quotation, but does not attempt a statistically rigorous quantitative characterization of the behaviour it documents.

item.title: Understanding Generative AI Use in Programming MOOCs: The Role of Course Context and Learner Characteristics
item.description: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, such as ChatGPT and code-completion assistants, raises questions about how learners integrate these tools into learning activities, particularly in MOOCs that attract diverse participant populations. This study examines the use of GenAI in two programming MOOCs taught in Estonian that differ in duration, workload, topic complexity, and assignment volume: About Programming (4 weeks, 26 expected hours, n = 187) and Introduction to Programming (8 weeks, 78 expected hours, n = 182). Post-course questionnaire data were analyzed using non-parametric statistical methods to examine self-reported adoption, usage frequency, and purposes of GenAI use across courses and learner backgrounds. The results show that GenAI adoption was widespread in both MOOCs, with no statistically significant differences by gender, age, education level, or prior programming experience. However, participants in the longer, more extensive MOOC reported significantly higher usage frequency and were more likely to use GenAI for debugging and idea generation. Reported usage frequency for code explanation and debugging was also higher in the longer course. Exploratory analyses found limited relationships between GenAI use and learning-related outcomes. The findings suggest that course context may play a greater role than learner characteristics in shaping how GenAI tools are used. These results provide implications for instructional design and guidance in programming education.

item.title: Large Language Models and Augmented Democracy
item.description: Artificial intelligence enables computational agents to represent political preferences and take part in collective decision-making. In this thesis, I investigate the opportunities and challenges of digital twins (DTs) based on Large Language Models (LLMs) as intermediaries in augmented democracy, focusing on individual preference representation, collective representation of political organizations, and the vulnerability of those representations to attackers. First, using data from an online experiment in Brazil, I examine whether personalized DTs can predict citizens' preferences for unseen policy proposals. Second, I extend the DT framework from individuals to political organizations. Using Swiss parliamentary data, I build topic-specific knowledge graphs from lawmakers' legislative records and connect them to LLM-based lawmaker agents, which are organized into party-level DTs representing collective positions. Agentic deliberation among these agents tests whether aggregated party representations capture a broader range of intra-party perspectives than official party communications. Finally, I study the vulnerability and robustness of LLM-mediated deliberation against prompt-injection attacks that amplify viewpoints, suppress opinions, or redirect consensus. Using data from a 2023 deliberative experiment in the United Kingdom, I analyze how attack effectiveness varies with the distribution of opinions and rhetorical strategies, and evaluate a pipeline combining injection detection, structured opinion representations, and reinforcement learning to improve resistance. These findings characterize the opportunities and challenges of LLM-based digital twins in augmented democracy, stressing accurate preference representation, faithful aggregation, and robustness to strategic interaction.

item.title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
item.description: Generative AI weakens the link between assessed performance and the cognitive processes that educational work is expected to reflect. This paper examines observable traces of those processes in a sample of 150 student-AI conversations. The analysis uses the concept of epistemic ownership as an interpretive framework, focusing on three dimensions that can become visible in interaction: Direction, Integration, and Evaluation. The results show that similar assessed performance can coexist with substantially different observable patterns of cognitive participation. Assignment scores therefore provide information about assessed outcomes but do not recover how cognitive work was distributed between student and AI during the interaction. The study provides an empirical basis for asking how assessment should incorporate evidence about cognitive process, rather than relying exclusively on the quality of the resulting product.

item.title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
item.description: AI can help adults produce plausible workplace artefacts while leaving their independent reasoning difficult to inspect. LearnAdapt Praxis addresses this design problem through a five-stage learning workspace: Frame, Learn, Build, Validate and Transfer. The application stores an initial response, versioned specifications, coaching records, validation observations, a separate transfer response and facilitator feedback. Project-level server controls restrict coaching, access to earlier work and learner export during an active transfer attempt; they do not establish that a learner avoided assistance outside the application. This technical report describes the implemented architecture and evaluates selected workflow, authority, failure-recovery and provenance properties. A reproducible synthetic rehearsal exercised 120 serial project episodes across three fictional workplace contexts and four injected provider conditions. All 3,990 recorded checks met their specified expectations. The resulting records contained 240 specification versions, 1,200 activity events and 60 stored synthetic hints; 60 injected provider failures produced no fabricated hints. Separate authentication regressions exposed and resolved a session-expiry defect, and limited staging and production checks verified account access and live model connectivity. The evidence supports the tested engineering properties of the recorded release. It does not establish learning gains, model-output quality, unaided assessment validity, population usability or production capacity. The contribution is an implemented arrangement for separating assisted work, project-level assistance withdrawal and inspectable evidence, accompanied by executable tests and an explicit account of what remains to be validated with adult learners.

item.title: Social bot detection in the age of ChatGPT: Challenges and opportunities
item.description: We present a comprehensive overview of the challenges and opportunities in social bot detection in the context of the rise of sophisticated AI-based chatbots. By examining the state of the art in social bot detection techniques and the more salient real-world application to date, we identify gaps and emerging trends in the field, with a focus on addressing the unique challenges posed by AI-generated conversations and behaviors. We suggest potentially promising opportunities and research directions in social bot detection, including (i) the use of generative agents for synthetic data generation, testing and evaluation; (ii) the need for multimodal and cross-platform detection based on network and behavioral signatures of coordination and influence; (iii) the opportunity to extend bot detection to non-English and low-resource language settings; and, (iv) the room for development of collaborative, federated learning detection models that can help facilitate cooperation between different organizations and platforms while preserving user privacy.

item.title: Architecture Without an Architect? Global Governance of Artificial Intelligence in a Divided World
item.description: Artificial intelligence presents an unusually difficult problem for global governance. The technology develops rapidly, crosses borders easily, and is shaped by actors whose resources and capabilities may rival those of states. Yet international responses remain fragmented, unevenly representative, and overwhelmingly non-binding. The challenge is therefore not simply to identify appropriate rules or institutions, but to understand who has the capacity and incentive to create, enforce, and adapt them. This review essay examines these questions through Matthijs Maas's Architectures of Global AI Governance. Maas offers an ambitious framework for thinking about AI governance through the lenses of sociotechnical change, governance disruption, and regime complexity. His account usefully resists both technological determinism and the search for a single institutional blueprint, emphasizing instead the possibilities of a fragmented and evolving governance architecture. The essay argues, however, that institutional design cannot be separated from the distribution of power. Maas frequently invokes what "we" should do about AI, but that collective subject obscures important differences among states, international institutions, and technology companies. States retain formidable powers over markets, infrastructure, strategic inputs, and firms themselves. At the same time, many consequential decisions about frontier AI - what is built, how quickly, with what safeguards, and when it is released - are concentrated within a small number of private companies. The central problem of global AI governance may therefore be less architecture without an architect than an emerging architecture shaped by multiple actors possessing different forms of power, divergent incentives, and no common set of plans.

item.title: Designing Adaptive Affective Chatbots for Online Learning: Trade-offs Between User Control, Automation, and Transparency
item.description: Online students often face emotional challenges such as frustration, isolation, and fluctuating motivation, which can hinder sustained engagement in online learning. While affective chatbots have shown promise in healthcare and wellness, most learning support chatbots focus primarily on cognitive assistance with limited attention to learners' emotional and motivational experiences. In this work, we investigate how adaptive affective chatbot support can be designed for online learning through an iterative design process. Through a mixed-methods needfinding study (n=38), we identified substantial variation in how learners respond to affective support, with no single strategy universally preferred. This led us to develop three adaptive design alternatives: user-controlled, AI-driven, and hybrid co-controlled adaptation, and examine key trade-offs between automation, transparency, and user control. A final evaluation (n=25) showed that 88% of participants favored the adaptive hybrid design over a non-adaptive alternative, highlighting the value of balancing transparency, user control, and interaction simplicity. We discuss design implications for adaptive affective chatbot systems in emotionally challenging online learning contexts.

item.title: When the Judge Acts: Auditing VLM-Guided Image Selection on Culturally Situated Prompts
item.description: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly act as judges that pick the best of several generated images, so their choices decide what users see. Such judges are usually validated by score agreement with human ratings, not by the images they return. We audit VLM judges as decision-makers: on 300 culturally situated prompts, we compare the returned image with human ratings the judge never sees and with random choice from the same candidates, and repeat every decision with the candidates reordered. A 4B-parameter judge barely beats random and falls short of a CLIP similarity baseline. It picks the first image shown in 49% of calls (chance: 28%), and reordering changes its choice on 60% of prompts. For this judge, agreement across orders is informative: decisions that survive reordering are much better than random, whereas agreement with a weaker second judge keeps the wrong ones. An 8B judge shows almost no position bias and outperforms CLIP, yet for it the same filter mostly discards good decisions. Agreement helps only when it targets the judge's failure mode, so filters must be re-audited whenever the judge changes. The 4B judge's slight rise in stereotype ratings is no longer detectable after aggregating across orders or with the larger judge.

item.title: Judgement in the Age of Jev: From Evaluation Scarcity to Evaluation Abundance
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence has reduced the cost of producing plausible symbolic artefacts, leading recent organisation scholarship to identify evaluation and discernment as constraints under conditions of production abundance. This perspective examines a further possibility: that machine evaluation itself becomes inexpensive enough to be deployed routinely and at scale. The investigation is prompted by Jev, TypeSafe AI's specialised model for typed probabilistic decisions. TypeSafe explicitly invokes William Stanley Jevons to argue that lower-cost machine intelligence can unlock previously uneconomic uses. Treating this as a technological provocation rather than an established empirical result, the article formulates a conditional Jevons hypothesis for machine evaluation: sufficiently large reductions in the total marginal cost of usable machine evaluation may increase its organisational consumption where latent demand is substantial and complementary costs do not dominate.
